intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. The notes under each slide explain it, give you something to remember and warn you where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, test yourself with the questions, and write your own notes in the margins.

sections.title: Foundations: Identity, Structure & Intersectionality
sections.big_idea: A social margin is a **structural position** produced by institutions and compounding across identities, so the diagnosis decides the programme.
in_plain_words: Social margins are positions where institutions, laws and cultural norms produce systematically worse outcomes for people because of who they are. Caste, tribe, religion, gender, sexuality, disability, region and language all act as vectors, and they rarely act alone. The margin belongs to the structure and describes a relationship, so it never names a trait of persons.

The conceptual toolkit helps you sort what you see: ascribed or achieved, visible or invisible, identity or structure. Crenshaw's intersectionality says the harm at an intersection exceeds the sum of single-axis harms. For practitioners the test is concrete: **who sits at the sharpest intersection, and is the design built for them?**

key_terms.meaning: Structural position producing systematically worse outcomes.
Assigned at birth, such as caste or indigeneity.
Identities compound into harm beyond their sum.
Fraser's two kinds of justice; both are needed.
Chakravarti's term for caste and gender made together.

worked_example.title: Diagnose before you prescribe
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an agency designs a women's livelihoods programme for upper-caste, literate women in plains districts.
steps: Ask the deck's test: who sits at the sharpest intersection of the identities involved?
Name the groups the design leaves out: Dalit, Muslim, Adivasi, disabled and trans women.
Choose the diagnosis. As 'diversity', the fix is an awareness campaign; as structure, it redistributes land, capital, education, representation and dignity.
Redesign for the sharpest intersection, and the gap stops compounding.
worked_example.answer: The design serves the dominant member of the named group; treat the margin as structure and redesign for the sharpest intersection.

mistakes: Treating marginalisation as diversity to be celebrated, which produces awareness campaigns and no redistribution.
Designing for 'women' or 'Dalits' as one block, which serves the dominant member of the group.
Running 'just work harder' framings on ascribed identities, which the structure makes unfit.
Addressing identity alone, or structure alone. The first risks celebration without redistribution, the second erases voice.

recall.q: What is a social margin, in the working definition?
recall.a: A structural position where institutional design, norms and power produce systematically worse outcomes for people based on ascribed identities, often in combination.

recall.q: Who coined intersectionality, and when?
recall.a: Kimberlé Crenshaw, in 1989.

recall.q: What does Chakravarti's 'Brahmanical patriarchy' name?
recall.a: The structural co-production of caste and gender.

recall.q: What is the difference between ascribed and achieved identity?
recall.a: Ascribed is assigned at birth; achieved is attainable through life choices.

recall.q: Why does the definition matter for programmes?
recall.a: The diagnosis dictates the prescription: diversity brings awareness campaigns, structure brings redistribution.

sections.title: Caste: Origins, Theory & the Long History
sections.big_idea: Caste has a **long, layered and contested history** that no single origin story captures, and it persists across religions.
in_plain_words: We have textual evidence from roughly 1500 BCE, archaeological and genetic evidence of migrations and mixing, and rival scholarly readings. What is settled is that caste has existed for at least two millennia. Texts like the Purusha Sukta and the Manusmriti are normative projects, and they give no record of how ordinary people lived.

Untouchability is the cruellest construction and persists despite Article 17. Srinivas described Sanskritisation as limited group mobility, which critics say accepts hierarchy. Bhakti, Sant, Sufi and Buddhist traditions challenged caste for centuries, and caste has reproduced itself in Sikhism, Christianity, Islam and Jainism. **Conversion is no sufficient exit.**

events.what: Vedic period; varna in the Purusha Sukta

diagram.caption: the deck's rough chronology of caste

key_terms.meaning: Four-fold ranking first named in the Purusha Sukta.
Graded practices treating communities as ritually polluting.
Lower castes adopting upper-caste ritual to claim status.
Numerous, land-owning caste controlling village politics.
Ambedkarite Buddhism; about 87% of Indian Buddhists.

worked_example.title: What 80% of 565 villages means
worked_example.setup: The deck cites Shah, Mander, Thorat and others (2006): in a survey of 565 villages across 11 states, 80% reported some untouchability practice.
steps: Convert the percentage into a count: 565 × 0.8 = 452 villages.
Check what remains: 565 − 452 = 113 villages reported none.
State the finding as the deck does: practices were still operating in most surveyed villages.
Pair it with Article 17: abolition is necessary but falls short.
worked_example.answer: About 452 of 565 villages reported some practice, so legal abolition has not ended it.

mistakes: Telling a single origin story, whether 'caste arrived in 1500 BCE' or 'caste was invented by the British'.
Reading the Dharmashastra as a description of daily life when it is a normative project.
Calling Sanskritisation liberation. The critique is that it changes position inside the hierarchy.
Presenting bhakti and Sant figures only as 'Hindu reformers', which flattens radical critiques.

recall.q: What is the deck's honest answer on caste origins?
recall.a: They are contested; the evidence supports a long, layered history of at least two millennia.

recall.q: What does Article 17 say?
recall.a: Untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden.

recall.q: Who coined Sanskritisation, and what did it describe?
recall.a: M.N. Srinivas (1952), the process of lower castes adopting upper-caste rituals, dress and diet to claim higher status.

recall.q: Name two traditions that challenged caste before the modern period.
recall.a: Any two of: Buddhism, Jainism, Lingayats, bhakti poets, Sufi orders, Sant traditions.

recall.q: Which groups does the SC list currently exclude?
recall.a: Dalit Christians and Muslims.

sections.title: Anti-Caste Thought: Phule, Ambedkar, Periyar
sections.big_idea: Anti-caste thought is **plural**: Phule, Ambedkar and Periyar led it, but a wider, multi-regional tradition came first and runs beside them.
in_plain_words: Phule founded schools and the Satyashodhak Samaj, linking caste, gender and education. Ambedkar combined movement, law and scholarship, from the Mahad Satyagraha to the Constitution, and argued in Annihilation of Caste that caste must be destroyed at its roots. Periyar fused anti-caste critique with atheism, women's liberation and Tamil politics for mass mobilisation.

The standard syllabus collapses this into Ambedkar alone, but Thass, Narayana Guru, Ayyankali, Varma, Mangoo Ram and women leaders worked decades earlier. The Gandhi-Ambedkar debate marks the defining disagreement, and later movements range from the Dalit Panthers to Dalit literature. Use **three lenses**: structural, cultural and intersectional.

key_terms.meaning: Phule's 1873 Society of Truth-Seekers.
1932 agreement on reserved seats in joint electorates.
Periyar's 1925 movement; later Dravidar Kazhagam.
Coalition of SC, ST, OBC and minorities.
Reads caste as relations of land, labour, capital.

worked_example.title: Check the 20-year forecast
worked_example.setup: Annihilation of Caste (1936) concludes that Ambedkar will not die a Hindu. The deck calls this a 20-year forecast of his 1956 conversion.
steps: Take the year of the speech: 1936.
Take the year of the conversion at Nagpur: 1956.
Compare with the Phule schools: the girls' school (1848) and the 'untouchables' school (1851) are 1851 − 1848 = 3 years apart.
worked_example.answer: The forecast spans 20 years, matching the deck's description.

mistakes: Presenting anti-caste thought as Ambedkar alone and erasing predecessors.
Softening the Gandhi-Ambedkar disagreement, as many textbooks have.
Reading Periyar as an academic text. His writing aimed at mass mobilisation in Tamil.
Using one lens only. A pure cultural lens misses land, and a pure intersectional lens without the others becomes empty pluralism.

recall.q: What did Phule's Gulamgiri (1873) dedicate itself to?
recall.a: The American abolitionists.

recall.q: Why did the Annihilation of Caste speech never get delivered?
recall.a: The Mandal asked Ambedkar to remove sections and he refused.

recall.q: What did the Poona Pact of 1932 provide?
recall.a: Reserved seats in joint electorates.

recall.q: What did Periyar add to anti-caste critique?
recall.a: He fused it with anti-Brahminism, atheism, women's liberation and Tamil cultural nationalism.

recall.q: Name the three lenses for anti-caste analysis.
recall.a: Structural or material, cultural or ideological, and intersectional.

sections.title: Caste, Colonialism & the Census
sections.big_idea: Colonial counting **hardened and classified caste** without inventing it, and those categories still frame reservation and the census debate.
in_plain_words: The British did not invent caste, but the census from 1871 forced fluid identities into fixed boxes, and Risley's 1901 ranking set communities competing for rank. Caste associations petitioned for reclassification, and the Criminal Tribes Act of 1871 hardened caste by law, notifying whole communities as hereditary criminals.

The South Indian non-Brahmin movement took a distinct path, and independence kept colonial categories, from the 1936 SC list to the Constitution. Today the question is whether to hold a caste census. The deck notes that the absence of data after 1931 for non-SC/ST groups is **a continuing political choice**, and the 2025 decision to enumerate caste in the next Census reverses it.

right.title: Under colonial governance
items: Caste codified in law and records

key_terms.meaning: Counting that fixes identities into categories.
1901 attempt to rank castes by social precedence.
1871 law notifying communities as hereditary criminals.
Name given after the Act's 1952 repeal.
Caste data collected but never publicly released.

worked_example.title: Add up Bihar's 2023 survey
worked_example.setup: The deck gives the Bihar caste survey shares: OBC 27.1%, EBC 36.0%, SC 19.7% and ST 1.7%.
steps: Add the first two: 27.1 + 36.0 = 63.1.
Add the SC share: 63.1 + 19.7 = 82.8.
Add the ST share: 82.8 + 1.7 = 84.5.
The remainder is 100 − 84.5 = 15.5, which matches the deck's forward or unreserved castes.
worked_example.answer: The four named groups make up 84.5%; the forward or unreserved castes are the remaining 15.5%.

mistakes: Saying the British invented caste. The calibrated claim is that they hardened, classified and pan-Indianised it.
Treating the missing post-1931 caste data as a technical oversight.
Forgetting that Denotified Tribes often fall outside SC, ST and OBC categories.
Presenting southern caste politics as a copy of the north.

recall.q: In which year was Risley's ranking by social precedence attempted?
When was the last full caste enumeration?
How many people had been notified under the Criminal Tribes Act by 1947?
recall.a: About 13 million across some 200 communities.

recall.q: What did the 1921 Communal Government Order provide?
recall.a: Reservation in education and employment in the Madras Presidency.

recall.q: What did the Union Cabinet decide on 30 April 2025?
recall.a: To include caste enumeration in the next Census.

sections.title: Constitution, Article 17 & Reservations
sections.big_idea: The Constitution abolishes untouchability and treats reservation as **an instrument of equality**, governed by thick case-law and uneven results.
in_plain_words: Articles 14, 15, 16, 17, 25(2)(b), 46, 338 and 341–342 form the framework, and they differ in force: some are rights, some enable reservation, one is a directive principle. Reservation has a long history from princely Mysore to 2019, and today's Union quotas of SC 15%, ST 7.5%, OBC 27% and EWS 10% total about 59.5%.

Mandal, Indra Sawhney and the EWS case set the doctrine: a 50% ceiling, the creamy layer and the 2022 ruling that the ceiling is not inflexible. The PoA Act gives enhanced penalties but low conviction rates. Evidence shows gains at entry level and gaps at senior levels. **Reservation is the instrument of equality under structural inequality**, and its design still has to be tested.

diagram.note: without EWS the total was 49.5%, under the 50% ceiling

key_terms.meaning: Abolishes untouchability; self-executing and punishable.
Affluent OBCs excluded from quota benefits.
The 50% cap on total reservation (1992).
Economically Weaker Sections; 10% under the 103rd Amendment.
Prevention of Atrocities Act, 1989.

worked_example.title: Test the 50% ceiling
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's Union-level quotas: SC 15%, ST 7.5%, OBC 27% and EWS 10%.
steps: Before EWS: 15 + 7.5 + 27 = 49.5, just under the ceiling.
Compare with the 50% cap: 59.5 − 50 = 9.5 points above it.
Janhit Abhiyan (2022) held by 3:2 that the ceiling is not inflexible.
worked_example.answer: The total is 59.5%, 9.5 points above the Indra Sawhney ceiling, which the 2022 majority accepted.

mistakes: Treating all constitutional articles as equal in force. Some enable, one is a directive principle, Article 17 is self-executing.
Quoting the 50% ceiling as absolute after Janhit Abhiyan.
Assuming a strong statute means strong outcomes. Conviction rates under the PoA Act are low.
Reading reservation success from entry-level numbers alone, ignoring faculty and senior posts.

recall.q: What did Indra Sawhney (1992) introduce besides the 50% cap?
recall.a: The creamy layer concept for OBCs.

recall.q: What did Davinder Singh (2024) permit?
recall.a: State sub-categorisation within SCs, by a 7-judge bench.

recall.q: What annual income threshold applies to EWS?
recall.a: Below ₹8 lakh gross, with certain land-holding limits.

recall.q: What happened after Subhash Kashinath Mahajan in 2018?
recall.a: Dalit protests followed, and Parliament passed an amendment restoring the original framework.

recall.q: Name one reason reservation penetrates senior posts less.
recall.a: Any of: creamy-layer dominance, little post-entry support, hostile work cultures, no private-sector reservation.

sections.title: Caste & the Economy
sections.big_idea: Caste organises land, labour, capital and mobility, so it is **an economic structure** with efficiency costs as well as equity costs.
in_plain_words: Caste shapes who owns land, who hires whom, who borrows, who marries whom and therefore who inherits. Land ownership remains caste-stratified despite reform. Wage studies find a caste gap that survives controls, and audit experiments show discrimination in hiring. Manual scavenging shows that a legal ban leaves the labour structure in place.

Business networks are caste-defined, and reservation does not reach the private market. Mobility across caste lines is slow but real, with education moving faster than jobs, wages and assets. Bihar's 2023 survey gave numbers to the debate. Ambedkar's point is that caste is a division of labourers, and **markets then run on top of a fixed allocation**.

diagram.caption: four channels through which caste acts on the economy

key_terms.meaning: Wage gap that survives controls for education and region.
Matched applications testing hiring discrimination.
Handling human excreta; prohibited since 1993.
Ambedkar's term for graded, hereditary workers.
Bihar sub-category within SC.

worked_example.title: Read the audit study
worked_example.setup: Illustrative base rate: suppose upper-caste applicants receive 30 call-backs per 100 applications. The deck's study found upper-caste applicants got about 1.5 times the Dalit rate and 3 times the Muslim rate, for the same CV.
steps: Dalit rate: 30 ÷ 1.5 = 20 call-backs per 100.
Muslim rate: 30 ÷ 3 = 10 call-backs per 100.
Compare the two groups: 20 ÷ 10 = 2, so Dalit applicants received twice the Muslim rate.
The CV was matched, so the difference comes from the name.
worked_example.answer: 20 and 10 call-backs per 100 against 30 for upper-caste applicants, on identical CVs.

mistakes: Treating caste only as a cultural variable in growth models.
Assuming land reform solved landlessness. The deck lists zamindari abolition as the main broad success.
Reading the official manual-scavenger count as complete. Survey definitions exclude septic-tank workers.
Expecting reservation to reach the private market.

recall.q: What share of SC rural households have no agricultural land or only homestead land?
recall.a: About 58%.

recall.q: What did Thorat and Attewell test?
recall.a: Matched job applications with Hindu upper-caste, Dalit and Muslim names sent to 548 private-sector advertisements.

recall.q: Which Act first prohibited manual scavenging?
recall.a: The Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993.

recall.q: What share of marriages stay within jati?
recall.a: 95% or more (IHDS-2).

recall.q: Why does shrinking public employment have caste consequences?
recall.a: Public-sector jobs are the most caste-equal large employer, so their loss closes a mobility ladder.

sections.title: Caste & Violence
sections.big_idea: Caste violence is **a pattern that punishes assertion**, and registered figures are a floor while convictions stay low.
in_plain_words: NCRB figures count registered crimes, so they reflect incidence and registration practice together, and under-reporting is severe. Documented cases from Kilvenmani to Hathras show the pattern. Triggers include material assertion, symbolic assertion, inter-caste relationships, reservation backlash, sexual violence and land conflict, and the common thread is assertion that disrupts an unspoken settlement.

Honour violence, the criminal-justice bottleneck and violence against women are the main strands. The 2015 amendment to the PoA Act added time-bound trials and special courts, yet gaps remain. Sexual violence against Dalit and Adivasi women works as collective punishment. The practitioner's question is **what assertion was being punished**, and what that shows about the structure.

diagram.caption: where cases drop out of the criminal justice pipeline

key_terms.meaning: A floor for incidence, shaped by registration practice.
Dalit or Adivasi claim that disrupts the settlement.
Violence over inter-caste marriage; under-counted.
Supreme Court guidelines protecting inter-caste couples.
Courts the 2015 amendment made mandatory.

worked_example.title: Read the SC crime trend
worked_example.setup: The deck gives registered crimes against SCs: about 47,000 in 2014 and about 57,500 in 2022.
steps: As a share of the 2014 figure: 10,500 ÷ 47,000 = 0.22, about 22%.
The slide also says per-population rates rose roughly 35%. A rate cannot outpace the count if the population grows, so check that figure at its source.
Remember the rise mixes real incidence and improved registration.
worked_example.answer: A rise of about 22% in registered cases, which mixes incidence and registration; treat the 35% rate with caution.

mistakes: Reading a rise in registered crime as a rise in incidence.
Asking what provoked the violence. The more useful question is what assertion was being punished.
Treating atrocities as isolated tragedies when they form a pattern.
Assuming a stronger Act fixes outcomes. Implementation gaps remain wide.

recall.q: Roughly how many crimes against SCs did NCRB record in 2022?
recall.a: About 57,500.

recall.q: Name three of the six triggers of atrocities.
recall.a: Any three of: material assertion, symbolic assertion, inter-caste relationship, reservation backlash, sexual violence, land and resource conflict.

recall.q: What did Shakti Vahini v Union of India (2018) provide?
recall.a: Binding guidelines including special cells, safe houses and FIR registration.

recall.q: What time limit did the PoA Act's 2015 amendment set for trials?
recall.a: 60 days from charge-sheet.

recall.q: What happened in Hathras in 2020?
recall.a: A young Dalit woman died after alleged gangrape, and a police-administered cremation against the family's wishes drew national outrage.

sections.title: Caste & Education
sections.big_idea: Education gaps have **narrowed but not closed**, and they are widest at the top: faculty, elite institutions and the coaching gate.
in_plain_words: Caste-disaggregated data show large gaps that have narrowed over decades. SC and ST higher-education enrolment has risen, partly because reservation expanded, but dropout is higher at every school transition, scholarship arrears recur and caste is felt in classrooms. Rohith Vemula's death in 2016 brought discrimination in elite universities into national conversation.

UGC cells and regulations exist, yet implementation lags and faculty hiring is diluted by roster disputes. Coaching for high-stakes exams costs more than most SC/ST families can pay, and public schemes show that targeted investment works at limited scale. Faculty representation is the most resistant gap, and Ambedkar's call to **educate, agitate, organise** treats education as the work itself.

diagram.caption: the gap widens as you move up the ladder

key_terms.meaning: Gross Enrolment Ratio in higher education.
UGC-mandated body in higher education institutions.
Eklavya Model Residential Schools for STs.
Private exam preparation, stratified by caste and class.
Posting system that decides reserved faculty positions.

worked_example.title: Measure the enrolment gaps
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's AISHE 2021–22 figures: SC GER about 25% (up from about 13% in 2010), ST about 21% and the all-India average about 28%.
steps: SC gain since 2010: 25 − 13 = 12 percentage points.
SC gap to the all-India average: 28 − 25 = 3 points.
ST gap to the all-India average: 28 − 21 = 7 points.
The ST gap is the larger one, and faculty gaps remain wider still.
worked_example.answer: SC enrolment gained 12 points and sits 3 below the average; ST sits 7 below.

mistakes: Reading higher enrolment as equality. The gradient is steepest at the highest levels.
Counting hostels and scholarships as a fix when payments arrive late.
Treating Equal Opportunity Cells as working because they exist on paper.
Concluding that coaching schemes cannot work. The slide says the constraint is scale and funding.

recall.q: What did Hoff and Pandey (2006) find?
recall.a: Identical-ability children perform worse on tests when caste is publicly disclosed beforehand.

recall.q: When did Rohith Vemula die?
recall.a: 17 January 2016.

recall.q: What do the UGC regulations of 2012 require of institutions?
recall.a: Mandatory Equal Opportunity Cells, with SC/ST cells holding grievance redressal authority.

recall.q: What does a coaching fee of ₹1.5 to 3 lakh a year do?
recall.a: It excludes most SC/ST families.

recall.q: Which Ambedkar speech gives the 'educate, agitate, organise' call?
recall.a: His address to the All India Depressed Classes Conference, Nagpur, 18 July 1942.

sections.title: Caste, Gender & Sexuality
sections.big_idea: Endogamy is the **master mechanism**: caste reproduces through marriage, which controls women's sexuality, and Dalit, Adivasi and Pasmanda women stand differently.
in_plain_words: Chakravarti's Brahmanical patriarchy says caste hierarchy and gender control interlock, with women's sexuality managed to preserve caste boundaries. Dalit feminism answered that mainstream feminism could not theorise Dalit women's lives, and Adivasi and Pasmanda women add standpoints of their own. Women's labour force participation also varies by caste.

About 95% of marriages stay within jati, so caste survives changes in occupation, residence and education. Caste also shapes sexual access and queer politics, from the Devadasi system to Dalit queer organising. Ambedkar's 1916 argument makes endogamy the central problem, and programmes that skip marriage and women's sexual autonomy **leave the engine intact**.

key_terms.meaning: Marriage within the group; caste's master mechanism.
Manusmriti's law of women's conduct.
Standpoint feminism of Dalit women, since the 1990s.
Religious-office tradition; abolished by state laws.
Women leaving field work as families gain mobility.

worked_example.title: What 95% within jati means
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: take 1,000 marriages and apply the IHDS-2 figure that about 95% stay within jati.
steps: Within jati: 1,000 × 0.95 = 950 marriages.
Crossing jati lines: 1,000 − 950 = 50 marriages.
The deck adds that most reported inter-caste marriages join adjacent sub-castes.
True Dalit-savarna marriage is under 5%, so fewer than 50 of the 1,000 would qualify.
worked_example.answer: About 950 stay within jati and 50 cross lines, of which fewer still cross the Dalit-savarna divide.

mistakes: Treating Brahmanical patriarchy as the only frame. Critics say it can over-textualise lived, regional, material domination.
Folding Adivasi feminism into Dalit feminism. The slide says they differ in many premises.
Counting any 'inter-caste' marriage as a break in endogamy when it joins adjacent sub-castes.
Reforming representation while leaving endogamy untouched.

recall.q: What does Brahmanical patriarchy name?
recall.a: The historical interlocking of caste hierarchy with gender control through endogamy.

recall.q: Why does Ambedkar call endogamy the central problem?
recall.a: Caste cannot be preserved except by it; every other feature rests on the marriage rule.

recall.q: Roughly what share of Indian marriages stay within jati?
recall.a: About 95% (IHDS-2).

recall.q: What did the 2018 Section 377 reading-down leave unaddressed?
recall.a: Caste in queer life.

recall.q: What did Tamil Nadu's 2009 amendment change?
recall.a: It removed the need for 'caste' on marriage certificates.

sections.title: Caste in the Diaspora & Workplaces
sections.big_idea: Caste travels with migrants and now meets **law, corporate policy and international forums**, where no caste-neutral position exists.
in_plain_words: South Asian migrants carry caste through marriage networks, religious institutions and workplaces. Cases such as Tirkey v Chandhok, Cisco and the Seattle ban show the legal frontier, and surveys in the US document discrimination in housing, education and tech. Reservation does not apply in the private sector, and HR teams are rarely equipped to handle caste claims.

India argues in international forums that caste is not race, while CERD treats descent-based discrimination as covered, which creates a bind. Some multinationals now name caste in policy. The strategic choice is between blindness and different forms of consciousness: **there is no caste-neutral position** in a caste-shaped society.

events.what: Cisco case; Apple adds caste to policy

key_terms.meaning: UN concept covering caste and similar systems.
International Convention on racial discrimination.
UK power to add caste; not yet activated.
Policy that ignores caste, assuming neutrality.
Policy that names caste and acts on it.

worked_example.title: Order the legal milestones
worked_example.setup: A colleague gives you four labels: Seattle ban, Cisco case, Tirkey v Chandhok, California SB 403.
steps: Start with the earliest: Tirkey v Chandhok, a UK tribunal, 2015.
Next comes the Cisco case, a US civil rights agency suit, from 2020.
Then Seattle in February 2023, the first US city to ban caste discrimination.
Last is California SB 403 (2023), passed by the legislature and vetoed by the Governor.

mistakes: Assuming caste-blind policy is neutral. In a caste-shaped market it reproduces existing patterns.
Treating the UK Equality Act as already covering caste. Section 9(5)(a) allows it and has not been activated.
Overlooking how India's international and domestic positions pull in different directions.
Adopting a corporate policy that names caste but gives investigators no caste-specific training.

recall.q: What did Equality Labs's 2018 survey cover?
recall.a: 1,500 South Asian Americans, documenting caste-based discrimination in several settings.

recall.q: Why is the diaspora debate also about the Indian state?
recall.a: Because governments choose whether to support, oppose as internal, or ignore international measures.

recall.q: Name three features of good corporate practice.
recall.a: Any three of: caste named explicitly, anonymous reporting, trained investigators, disaggregated metrics, protection from retaliation, engagement with Dalit networks.

recall.q: What does CERD General Recommendation 29 say?
recall.a: Descent-based discrimination is covered by ICERD; India contests this.

recall.q: What is the main argument against caste-blind organisations?
recall.a: In a caste-shaped market, blindness reproduces existing patterns and the dominant group's definition of merit is itself caste-shaped.

sections.title: Contemporary Debates
sections.big_idea: Each live debate pits **empirical evidence against political and constitutional limits**: who is counted, who benefits and who gets to exit.
in_plain_words: Reservation design is contested from several sides: Davinder Singh allows sub-categorisation within SCs, dominant agrarian castes demand quotas, and EWS applies an income test to a social remedy. The caste census, anti-conversion laws and the Pasmanda exclusion all turn on data and status, and private-sector reservation remains an open question.

Other debates widen the lens: Dalit capitalism, climate vulnerability, social media, Hindutva and Dalit politics, transnational organising and cultural production. The closing framing says the struggle now concerns how to dismantle a structure that has reorganised itself, and **caste analysis is a basic competence** for development work.

diagram.caption: fourteen slides, three families of debate

key_terms.meaning: Dividing SC benefits among sub-castes (Davinder Singh).
Affluent members excluded from quota benefits.
Inequality across groups, unlike household inequality.
Argument that markets give Dalits a path to mobility.
Lower-caste Muslims, about 85% of Muslims.

worked_example.title: Put the EWS threshold in scale
worked_example.setup: The EWS ceiling is ₹8 lakh of annual gross income. The Bihar survey in the deck used a line of ₹6,000 monthly income for Rajput, Bhumihar and Mahadalit families. The two measure different things, so compare them only for scale.
steps: Annualise the Bihar line: 6,000 × 12 = 72,000.
Write the EWS ceiling in rupees: 8 lakh is 800,000.
The EWS ceiling is about eleven times the annual value of the Bihar line, which fits the slide's point that it covers families well above median income.
worked_example.answer: About 11 times, which supports the critique that the threshold includes families well above the median.

mistakes: Treating sub-categorisation as settled. The Davinder Singh ruling leaves implementation to states.
Equating a dominant caste's economic distress with constitutional backwardness.
Conflating EWS with SC/ST/OBC reservation, which rest on different theories of why redistribution is owed.
Assuming caste data would settle the politics. It carries risks of sharper competition over fixed pools.

recall.q: What did Davinder Singh (2024) overrule?
recall.a: E.V. Chinnaiah (2005), which treated SCs as one homogeneous group.

recall.q: What was the vote in Janhit Abhiyan?
recall.a: 3:2 in favour of upholding the 10% EWS reservation.

recall.q: When did the Union Cabinet decide to include caste in the next Census?
recall.a: 30 April 2025.

recall.q: Which two states had enacted anti-conversion laws first?
recall.a: Odisha in 1967 and Madhya Pradesh in 1968.

recall.q: What does the Dalit capitalism debate ask?
recall.a: How much market expansion alone can do in a caste-segregated capital market, and what state action it also needs.

sections.title: The Other Vectors: A South Asian Survey
sections.big_idea: Tribe, religion, gender, sexuality, disability, language and class each have their own structure, and **none works alone**.
in_plain_words: The survey gives each vector a primer and a deeper data slide. Adivasi politics turns on land and autonomy, religion on communalism and minority rights, gender on care, property and violence. Sexuality and disability sit under rights frameworks that outrun implementation, language and region work through federalism, class compounds with caste, and migration exposes the citizen at the margin.

A practitioner's toolkit synthesises the course: diagnose the vectors in the room, disaggregate, read recognition with redistribution, centre affected voice, resist single-axis solutions and build for decades. The section closes with reading lists, glossaries and data checks. The common lesson is that **aggregate figures flatter the powerful** by hiding the margin.

key_terms.meaning: Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups; 75 flagged.
Free, prior, informed consent for tribal districts.
Disability arises from how society is organised.
Lists 22 recognised languages.
Political identity tied to region and language.

worked_example.title: Compare shares with burdens
worked_example.setup: Three comparisons from the deck's data slides.
steps: Adivasis are 8.6% of the population and bear about 40% of development-induced displacement: 40 ÷ 8.6 = 4.65 times their population share.
SC/ST are about 24% of the population and 36% of below-poverty-line households: 36 ÷ 24 = 1.5 times their share.
Women spend 297 minutes a day on unpaid work against 31 for men: 297 ÷ 31 = 9.6 times.
Each ratio shows why aggregates mislead.
worked_example.answer: About 4.65, 1.5 and 9.6 times, each showing a burden far above a population share or a comparison group.

mistakes: Treating 'tribal' as a synonym for rural poor. The politics centres on sovereignty over land and self-governance.
Using Sachar-era data as a ceiling for current numbers instead of a floor.
Quoting the Census disability figure as true prevalence when WHO estimates are far higher.
Offering English-only or Hindi-only programme materials in states and tribal areas.

recall.q: What does FRA implementation data show?
recall.a: About 2.4 million individual titles and about 123,000 community titles approved, but only about 13% of claimed community forest area recognised.

recall.q: What did NALSA 2014 recognise?
recall.a: Transgender persons as a third gender with full constitutional rights.

recall.q: What gap does the deck cite between Census 2011 and WHO on disability?
recall.a: 2.21% against 15 to 20%.

recall.q: How does the deck sum up class and caste?
recall.a: Class compounds with caste and does not replace it.

recall.q: Name two of the six steps in the practitioner's toolkit.
recall.a: Any two of: diagnose, disaggregate, read recognition with redistribution, centre affected voice, resist single-axis solutions, build for decades.

notes.2: Treat the agenda as a route. Section 1 frames the whole course, sections 2 to 11 follow caste in depth, and section 12 surveys the other vectors, with section 13 giving reading and a glossary. **Read section 1 first**, because every later section borrows its vocabulary.
notes.4: Memorise the definition by its verbs: institutions, norms and power produce worse outcomes for people because of who they are. The margin is a relational position inside a structure. The last paragraph carries the weight: **the diagnosis dictates the prescription**, so 'diversity' brings awareness campaigns and 'structure' brings redistribution.
notes.5: Six main axes and six that compound them. Learn the practitioner rule at the bottom: name the vector you work on and assume others are in the room. Programmes for 'women' or 'Dalits' without intersectional design tend to **serve the dominant member** of the named group.
notes.6: Six names anchor the course: Ambedkar and Phule on caste, Crenshaw on intersectionality, Spivak on representation, Young on five faces of oppression, Chakravarti on Brahmanical patriarchy. Pair each with the **one idea** it gave you, since later slides use them as shorthand.
notes.7: Three distinctions: ascribed or achieved, visible or invisible, identity or structure. The first shows why 'just work harder' is structurally unfit, since most marginalisation works on ascribed identity. The third warns that identity alone gives **celebration without redistribution**. Fraser's pair, recognition and redistribution, completes the set.
notes.8: Crenshaw's quote makes the central claim: the intersectional experience is greater than the sum of racism and sexism. The South Asian examples show harm at an intersection that single-axis programmes miss. Use the practitioner test: **who sits at the sharpest intersection, and is the design built for them?**
notes.10: Keep the layered timeline and resist neat stories. 'Caste arrived in 1500 BCE' and 'the British invented caste' each hold partial truths. The ancient DNA adds a marker: mixing slowed after about 100 CE, consistent with **caste marriage rules taking hold** around two millennia ago.
notes.11: The hymn ranks the four varnas anatomically, and the fifth group sits outside the body altogether. Most scholars read it as a later interpolation. Take the slide's warning with you: texts are normative projects and tell you **little about how ordinary people lived**.
notes.12: Untouchability is a graded set of practices, abolished by Article 17 yet documented to continue. The list covers water, seating, temples, residence, occupation and public services. In the 565-village survey, 80% reported some practice. Legal abolition is **necessary and still falls short**.
notes.13: Srinivas described group mobility: whole jatis adopting upper-caste ritual, dress and diet to claim status. Ambedkar and Omvedt answered that it accepts hierarchy. See how **one phenomenon looks different** from the top and the bottom, and read Srinivas beside Ambedkar and Phule.
notes.14: Caste critique has a long pre-modern history. Learn the list as a map: Buddhism and Jainism, Lingayats, bhakti poets, Sufi orders and Sant traditions. The warning concerns today's retelling, where radical critiques are **sanded down into Hindu reform**. The Kabir lines are a paraphrase.
notes.15: Buddhism is the first sustained anti-caste tradition: the Sangha admitted members of any caste, and worth came from conduct. Ambedkar's 1956 conversion, with roughly 380,000 followers, returned to it. The 2011 Census gives about 8.4 million Buddhists, **roughly 87% Navayana**.
notes.16: Read each row as doctrine against practice. Sikhism, Christianity, Islam, Jainism and Navayana Buddhism all hold equality in doctrine and show caste-like divisions in practice. The key lesson is that **conversion is no sufficient exit**. The slide adds that SC status currently excludes Dalit Christians and Muslims.
notes.18: Phule matters for institutions as well as ideas: the first school for girls (1848), the first for 'untouchables' (1851) and the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873). He wrote in Marathi for a non-Brahmin audience. His Aryan-invasion framework is contested but worked as an **ideological reversal**.
notes.19: Use the milestones as a timeline: Mahad 1927, Kalaram 1930, Poona Pact 1932, Labour Member 1942 to 46, Law Minister 1947 to 51, conversion 1956. Pair each writing with the movement around it. The Government of Maharashtra's 22-volume edition is **the canonical source**.
notes.20: Annihilation of Caste was an undelivered address: the Mandal asked for cuts, he refused, and he self-published. The argument runs that caste is a division of labourers, that it must be destroyed at its roots including scriptural sanction, and that dining and marriage are only **stepping stones**.
notes.21: Periyar fused anti-caste critique with anti-Brahminism, atheism, women's liberation and Tamil nationalism for mass mobilisation. Note the practical innovations: Self-Respect marriages without priests, and the journal Kudi Arasu. The slide calls his thought **more polemical and less academic** than Ambedkar's.
notes.22: Six figures the standard syllabus skips. Thass, Narayana Guru, Ayyankali, Phule's contemporaries, Varma and Mangoo Ram each worked in a different region. The slide's point is that the tradition is **plural, multi-regional and predates Ambedkar** by decades.
notes.23: Work down the table row by row: caste, untouchability, method, the Communal Award, Hindu identity and the village. The disagreement covers theory of change as well as tactics. Textbooks have softened it, so read the **Poona Pact correspondence** as the slide's corrective.
notes.24: Run the list as a timeline of organising and writing: the Panthers in 1972, BAMCEF and the BSP, NCDHR in 1998, the Bhim Army in 2015, and cinema. The literary list runs by language from Marathi to English. Note the caution on allies: **their standing is contested**, though some produce influential work.
notes.25: Three lenses, three questions: who owns what, which practices reproduce hierarchy, and how caste is gendered, regional and religious. The slide's verdict is the part to remember: **use all three**. Each alone misses something, whether land, everyday humiliation, or substance.
notes.27: The calibrated answer is that the British did not invent caste but helped harden, classify and pan-Indianise it. Pre-colonial caste was regional and plural, and colonial administration needed legible categories. The slide names the stakes: if caste is 'British', reform looks easy; if ancient and unchanging, impossible. **Current caste is a hybrid** needing several kinds of reform.
notes.28: The census forced fluid identities into fixed boxes, and communities responded by petitioning and reorganising to claim rank. Learn the dates: 1871 first, 1901 Risley's ranking, 1931 last full enumeration, 1941 collected but untabulated. The practitioner implication is that the missing later data is **a continuing political choice**.
notes.29: The Criminal Tribes Act designated whole communities as hereditary criminals, and by 1947 about 13 million people in some 200 communities had been notified. Repeal in 1952 produced the label Denotified Tribes, yet profiling continues. Read Mahasweta Devi and the **Budhan Theatre** for the contemporary struggle.
notes.30: Between 1881 and 1931 hundreds of caste associations petitioned for reclassification, usually upward: Yadavs, Lingayats, Nadars. Note what hardened: associations with offices and journals, pan-state identities, rewritten genealogies, caste hostels and respectability reforms. These formations **still shape electoral politics**, as the Yadav example shows.
notes.31: The southern path differs because an organised non-Brahmin movement began in the early twentieth century: the Justice Party, the 1921 Communal G.O. and the Self-Respect Movement. Tamil Nadu has 69% reservation by state law. Keep the tension in view: intermediate castes dominate the tradition, and Dalit movements ask **who actually benefits**.
notes.32: Read the timeline as layers: colonial counting at the base, then the 1936 SC list, the 1950 Constitution with Articles 17, 341 and 342, the 1955 and 1989 laws, Mandal in 1990 and EWS in 2019. The framework **inherited colonial categories**, and each step remains contested.
notes.33: Weigh both sides. For a caste census: reservation rests on 1931 data, Bihar's 2023 survey gave OBC 27.1%, EBC 36.0%, SC 19.7% and ST 1.7%, and welfare needs caste-disaggregated data. Against: reifying identities, more than 4,000 jatis, doubts over SECC quality. **The empirical case is strong and the political path contested.**
notes.35: Use the table as an index to the constitutional framework, and read the Force column. Articles 14 and 15(1) are rights, 15(4) and 16(4) enable reservation, Article 17 is self-executing and punishable, and Article 46 is a directive principle. The slide warns that the table is **not exhaustive**.
notes.36: Learn the long timeline from princely Mysore and Kolhapur through the 1921 Madras order, 1950, Kalelkar, Mandal, 1990 to 93, 2006 and 2019. Check the quotas yourself: 15 + 7.5 + 27 + 10 comes to about 59.5% at the Union level. State totals such as Tamil Nadu's 69% face **multiple challenges**.
notes.37: Mandal recommended 27% for OBCs using 11 indicators, and V.P. Singh's August 1990 decision triggered protests. The 27% was chosen so that total reservation stayed at 49.5%. Indra Sawhney upheld it and introduced the creamy layer. Politically, Mandal produced **a permanent shift in north Indian electoral politics**.
notes.38: Treat Indra Sawhney as the anchor: it upheld 27%, capped reservation at 50%, introduced the creamy layer and held that economic criteria alone cannot be the basis. Later rulings adjust it, from Nagaraj to Davinder Singh in 2024. Practitioners should **test proposals against case-law as well as politics**.
notes.39: The 103rd Amendment gave 10% to EWS households below ₹8 lakh gross income, outside the SC, ST and OBC quotas. Its novelty is reservation on purely economic grounds, breaching the 50% ceiling. Learn the 3:2 split: the majority held the ceiling is not inflexible, and the dissent called excluding the SC, ST and OBC poor **itself discriminatory**.
notes.40: The PoA Act lists specific acts committed against SC and ST members by non-SC/ST persons, such as forcible land occupation and public humiliation. The 2018 episode shows the cycle: a ruling diluted arrests, protests followed, Parliament restored the framework. With conviction rates near one-third, **implementation is the binding constraint**.
notes.41: Hold the numbers carefully. SC share in Group A central jobs is about 17.5% against a 16.6% population share, yet faculty share is about 3% and the senior-most Group A level about 6%. Reservation improved **entry-level access**, and it penetrated senior roles and the private sector less.
notes.42: Ambedkar's passage frames reservation as the instrument of equality under conditions of historic inequality. The practitioner lesson is a pair: the moral and constitutional case, and the empirical question of whether a specific design works. **Both are legitimate and neither cancels the other.**
notes.44: Caste shapes land, credit, hiring, marriage, residence and schooling, so treating it only as culture misses the economy, and treating the economy only as class misses the structure behind class formation. Use the six mechanisms as a checklist. The literature is large and its standard has risen with **audit experiments and RCTs**.
notes.45: Land is the clearest case. About 58% of SC rural households hold no agricultural land or only a homestead, and roughly 70% of operational holdings by area sit with upper and intermediate castes. Read the reform list as a scorecard: zamindari abolition worked broadly, while tenancy reform, ceilings, redistribution and Bhoodan **fell short**.
notes.46: Wage gaps survive controls for education, experience, occupation and region, and are largest in urban regular salaried and private corporate work, where merit claims are loudest. In the Thorat and Attewell audit of 548 advertisements, upper-caste applicants got about 1.5 times the Dalit call-back rate for **the same CV**.
notes.47: Manual scavenging has been prohibited since 1993 and strengthened in 2013, yet continues, almost exclusively among Dalit communities. The SECC 2011 recorded about 180,000 households, a likely under-count, partly because survey definitions exclude septic-tank workers. It is the clearest sign that **legal abolition is no social abolition**.
notes.48: Credit and capital follow caste networks. Dalit-owned firms are smaller and cluster in low-margin sectors, and trading communities hold hereditary trust networks that raise costs for newcomers. Reservation does not reach the private market, which the slide calls a serious gap. DICCI and Stand-Up India are two responses, and **Mudra's evaluation remains contested**.
notes.49: Mobility is slow but real. Schooling gaps are narrowing, occupation lags education, and wage and asset gaps narrow more slowly still, while 95% or more of marriages stay within jati. Public-sector jobs are the most caste-equal large employer, so **shrinking public employment closes a mobility ladder**.
notes.50: Bihar 2023 gives numbers to anchor the debate: EBC 36.0%, OBC 27.1% (63.1% together), SC 19.7% and forward castes 15.5%. It also shows poverty among 'upper' castes, proportionally lower than among SC/ST/EBC, and about 43% of Mahadalit families under ₹6,000. **Data re-opens arguments closed for lack of it.**
notes.51: Ambedkar's distinction is decisive: caste divides labourers as well as labour, and grades them one above another. In a normal division of labour workers can move by aptitude and demand; here the worker is fixed to the role at birth. For economists, caste carries **efficiency costs as well as equity costs**.
notes.53: Take NCRB numbers as a floor. About 57,500 crimes against SCs and 10,000 against STs were registered in 2022, but incidents often never reach an FIR, get registered under lesser sections, or need police action to invoke the PoA Act. Rising numbers reflect **both real incidence and registration practice**.
notes.54: Registered crimes against SCs rose from about 47,000 in 2014 to 57,500 in 2022. Four states account for over half of registrations, and conviction rates stay around 30 to 35%. Read the rise with care, because it mixes incidence and **improved registration**. ST cases run at one-fifth to one-sixth of SC cases.
notes.55: Use the table as a record of places and dates that forced national attention, from Kilvenmani in 1968 to Hathras in 2020. Note the legal pattern in several rows: acquittals on appeal, as at Kilvenmani and Tsundur. The slide calls the list **illustrative and not exhaustive**.
notes.56: Six triggers, one pattern: violence follows assertion. Material assertion, symbolic assertion, inter-caste relationships, reservation gains, sexual violence as punishment, and land conflicts each disturb an unspoken settlement. The reframing is the lesson: ask **what assertion was being punished** in place of asking what provoked the violence.
notes.57: Only about 5% of marriages cross jati lines, and when they do, especially a Dalit man with a non-Dalit woman, responses range from ostracism to murder. 'Honour killing' is under-counted in NCRB records. Learn the 2018 Shakti Vahini guidelines: special cells, safe houses and FIR registration. **Protection regimes still differ by state.**
notes.58: Walk down the bottleneck from FIR to appeal: refusals, watered-down charge-sheets, hostile witnesses, caste-linked investigators, under-resourced prosecutors, thin special courts and delayed appeals. The 2015 amendment added time-bound trials, special prosecutors, protection, exclusive courts and 26 new categories. The slide's conclusion is that **implementation gaps remain wide**.
notes.59: Sexual violence against Dalit and Adivasi women works as an instrument of caste discipline. NCRB 2022 recorded about 4,000 rapes against SC women and 1,000 against ST women, and independent assessments put true incidence many times higher. Five structural features compound the harm, including **pressure from the woman's own community** to withdraw.
notes.60: The Karamchedu testimony states the analytic point in survivors' own words: the violence punished a refusal of the assigned place. Caste violence is rarely spontaneous, so each incident is **a symptom of a pattern**. Ask the practitioner's question: what assertion was being punished, and what does it show about the structure you work in?
notes.62: SC enrolment in higher education (GER) is about 25%, up from about 13% in 2010, and ST is about 21% against an all-India 28%. The gap narrows partly because reservation pulls SC/ST enrolment up. Remember where it stays widest: faculty, STEM doctorates, private schooling and **coaching access**.
notes.63: Hoff and Pandey found that children of equal ability test worse when caste is publicly disclosed beforehand. Dropout is higher at every transition, and scholarship arrears recur. What works includes timely scholarships, hostels, KGBV, EMRS and bridge courses. Removing the gap needs **structural quality improvement as well as financial inclusion**.
notes.64: Rohith Vemula's death on 17 January 2016 brought caste in elite universities into national conversation. Read the documented patterns as a checklist: discipline, hostel allocation, slurs, dropout and suicide, faculty resistance and department networks. The slide names **Thorat's 2007 AIIMS committee report** as essential reading.
notes.65: UGC regulations require Equal Opportunity Cells, SC/ST cells, remedial classes and sensitisation, but implementation lags: notional cells, complaints funnelling back to the accused departments, retaliation. Faculty hiring is diluted by 'suitable candidate not found' and roster disputes. Know the **2018 roster judgment and the 2019 amendment** restoring the 200-point roster.
notes.66: High-stakes exams run through coaching that costs ₹1.5 to 3 lakh a year and works as an opaque pre-screening before reservation applies. Free schemes such as Super 30 and the Telangana Gurukul system partly offset it. The slide concludes that **targeted investment works**, with scale and consistent funding as the constraint.
notes.67: Faculty representation is the most resistant gap: SC professors about 3% at IITs, ST about 1%. The slide argues it matters beyond representation, because reading lists, mentorship, graduate admissions and peer-review networks all follow faculty's social location. **Gatekeeping at recruitment, promotion and awards remains caste-shaped.**
notes.68: Ambedkar's 1942 call puts education first, as the precondition for agitation and organisation. The slide argues that without it the other two collapse into resignation or futile confrontation, so the educational struggle is the work itself. For practitioners it is a long fight where **quality, faculty, dignity, mentorship and access move together**.
notes.70: Brahmanical patriarchy names the interlocking of caste hierarchy and gender control: women's sexuality and reproduction are managed to preserve caste boundaries. Endogamy is the master mechanism, and stridharma, sati, child marriage and limits on widow remarriage are its instruments. Keep the critique in mind: the framing can **over-textualise** lived, regional, material domination.
notes.71: Dalit feminism began from the recognition that mainstream feminism, built around upper-caste women's experience, could not theorise Dalit women's lives. Learn its contributions: the standpoint of those at the bottom, a critique of upper-caste feminism's blindness to caste, caste as **a primary dimension**, and a theory of Dalit women's labour.
notes.72: Adivasi and Pasmanda Muslim feminisms add two standpoints beyond the Dalit-savarna binary. Adivasi women face land alienation as a gendered crisis, and the slide says the standpoint should stay distinct from Dalit feminism. Pasmanda women face caste, gender and minority status together. Treating 'Indian women' as one category **misses those at the intersection**.
notes.73: Caste reproduces itself through marriage: about 95% of marriages stay within jati, and true Dalit-savarna marriage remains under 5%. Online matrimonial platforms have increased caste filtering. Endogamy is also the data infrastructure of caste, so reform aimed at representation while leaving it untouched **fights a losing battle**.
notes.74: Read this slide in two halves. The first covers sexual access and the Devadasi system, where anti-Devadasi laws drove the practice underground without adequate rehabilitation. The second covers queer caste politics: Dalit queer organisers call the mainstream movement heavily savarna, and the 2018 Section 377 reading-down **did not address caste**.
notes.75: Women's labour force participation varies sharply by caste: ST about 45%, SC about 25%, upper-caste below 20% in many surveys. Higher SC and ST participation partly reflects families that could not afford 'respectability'. Notice the **'Sanskritisation of labour'** as families gain mobility, and the entry points such as NREGS.
notes.76: Ambedkar's 1916 passage makes endogamy the central problem: caste cannot be preserved except by it. The slide's practical corollary is that a programme engaging caste without engaging marriage and women's sexual autonomy works on symptoms. **The hard work of caste reform runs through the family.**
notes.78: Migrants carry caste with them, from Trinidad and Mauritius to the UK and the US. Note the selection effects: post-1965 US migration was heavily upper-caste, and tech immigration built caste-stratified networks. Four cases mark the legal frontier: Tirkey v Chandhok, Cisco, Seattle and California's vetoed SB 403. In the UK, **Section 9(5)(a) is not yet activated**.
notes.79: Equality Labs's 2018 survey of 1,500 South Asian Americans found widespread caste-based discrimination, with two-thirds of Dalit respondents reporting mistreatment at work. Patterns include exclusion, denied mentorship, screening by name or alma mater, and blocked promotion. Reservation does not apply in the private sector, and **HR is unequipped** for caste claims.
notes.80: India argues internationally that caste and race are different things, so caste falls outside ICERD, while CERD General Recommendation 29 treats descent-based discrimination as covered. The 'two-position bind' is the slide's point: domestic remedies are said to work while external scrutiny is resisted. The **framing language** carries different weight in different rooms.
notes.81: A small but growing number of multinationals now name caste in anti-discrimination policy, triggered by Cisco, Seattle or employee organising. Use the good-practice list as a checklist: caste named explicitly, anonymous reporting, trained investigators, disaggregated metrics where legal, protection from retaliation, and engagement with **Dalit professional networks**.
notes.82: The table sets four strategies against their costs. Caste-blind avoids reifying caste, caste-conscious without quotas often produces marginal change, targets add accountability but are operationally complex, and private-sector reservation is the most direct but politically contested. The slide's verdict: **there is no caste-neutral position** in a caste-shaped society.
notes.84: Davinder Singh (2024) lets states sub-classify SCs, by a 6:1 majority of a 7-judge bench, overturning Chinnaiah. The empirical premise is that dominant SC sub-castes captured a disproportionate share of benefits. Hold the objections too: creamy layer for SC/ST runs against the structural argument, and sub-categorisation can **fragment Dalit coalitions**.
notes.85: Dominant agrarian castes, among them Marathas, Patidars, Jats, Kapus, Lingayats and Vokkaligas, have demanded reservation. The slide's puzzle: their economic distress is real, but their 'backwardness' in the constitutional sense is empirically weak, and the first **does not follow from the second**. Reservation has become the lens for all distributive demands.
notes.86: EWS critiques: the ₹8 lakh threshold was never empirically benchmarked, it covers families well above median income, the Sinho Commission recommended different criteria, and it overlaps with land-owning agrarian castes. The conceptual lesson: SC/ST/OBC reservation rests on structural discrimination and EWS on income alone, so **conflating them weakens both**.
notes.87: Here is where the caste-census debate stands: Bihar and Karnataka have enumerated, SECC 2011 data was never released, the 2021 Census was postponed, and the Union Cabinet decided in April 2025 on enumeration in the next Census, with a 1 March 2027 reference date. Weigh the uses against the risk of **sharper competition over fixed pools**.
notes.88: Anti-conversion laws, first passed in Odisha in 1967 and Madhya Pradesh in 1968, now operate in over a dozen states, often with advance notice and reversed burden of proof. Their caste edge: Dalits have converted to exit caste, and SC status is lost on conversion to Christianity or Islam, so these laws **raise the cost of caste exit through religion**.
notes.89: Read the Dalit capitalism debate as an empirical question under a structure. Prasad, Kamble and Babu argue that markets offer mobility; Deshpande answers that improvement followed public-sector reservation; Teltumbde says it absorbs leaders into the class system. The slide's question: given caste-segregated capital markets, **how much can markets alone do?**
notes.90: Climate burdens follow caste lines because SC and ST households are over-represented among landless labourers, sanitation, brick-kiln and informal workers, who face heat, floods and drought. The caste lens is largely missing from climate policy and finance. The slide invites practitioners to push for **caste-disaggregated vulnerability assessment**.
notes.91: Social media widened the space for Dalit voice, with first-person testimony and rapid mobilisation around Hathras, Una and Bhima-Koregaon. The same platforms carry coordinated casteist abuse, slow moderation, and moderators whose own caste shapes decisions. Hold both sides in view, since the dynamic is **double-edged**.
notes.92: The relationship between Hindutva and Dalit communities is neither simple inclusion nor simple exclusion: the BJP's Dalit vote share has risen since 2014 in several states, while the Ambedkarite tradition remains the most consistent counter-position. Use the five empirical questions as **a research agenda**, from welfare delivery to atrocity rates.
notes.93: Pasmanda means 'those left behind' and covers roughly 85% of Indian Muslims. Pasmanda politics challenges both Hindutva's view of Muslims as monolithic and Ashraf-led Muslim politics. The structural exclusion is the 1950 Order limiting SC status to Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists, with the **Balakrishnan Commission and Supreme Court petitions pending**.
notes.94: Anti-caste organising has gone transnational: IDSN coordinates 130+ groups across 18 countries, Equality Labs has been central to the Cisco litigation, the Seattle ordinance and SB 403, and UK campaigns press on Section 9. Alliances with Black liberation and Roma rights groups and the UN concept of descent-based discrimination give **comparative frameworks**.
notes.95: Cinema, music and art are where anti-caste politics meets popular consciousness. Tamil cinema since 2013–14 has centred Dalit characters with commercial success, which complicates older arguments about market viability. Use the director list as a viewing list, and note Stalin K.'s 2007 documentary India Untouched as **a foundational visual reference**.
notes.96: Weigh private-sector reservation. For: the private sector employs about 93% of Indian workers, audit studies show discrimination, and public-sector reservation built the Dalit middle class. Against: Article 16 does not bind private employers in current jurisprudence, plus competitiveness, enforcement and token-compliance worries. The slide judges a **statutory regime** more feasible than a constitutional amendment.
notes.97: The closing framing says the data has settled whether caste exists and the struggle is over how to dismantle a structure that has reorganised itself. The binding constraint is implementation, political will and imagination. For practitioners, **caste analysis is a basic competence**, comparable to gender or environment. The slide labels this the deck's own summary.
notes.99: Adivasi politics centres on sovereignty over land, language and self-governance, outside the varna scheme. Learn the constitutional layers: Schedules V and VI, PESA and FRA, and 75 PVTGs flagged for highest deprivation. The practitioner caution is the key line: ST status is no stand-in for general rural poverty, and conflating them tends to **dispossess people**.
notes.100: Religion works as both personal faith and political identity, and the colonial census institutionalised the Hindu/Muslim binary. Learn the constitutional framework by article: 25 to 28 on religious freedom, 29 and 30 on minority cultural and educational rights. Use the communal violence list as a benchmark: **each event rewrites the local margin**.
notes.101: Gender is the most universal vector and the most variably treated. The indicators give a quick profile, and the land figure, only 14% of agricultural landholders being women, shows the property gap. The practitioner reminder is the point: single-axis gender programming tends to serve **dominant-caste, Hindu, urban, able-bodied women**.
notes.102: South Asia holds old gender-non-conforming traditions alongside punitive colonial inheritances, Section 377 and the Criminal Tribes Act. Learn the legal sequence: NALSA 2014, Navtej Singh Johar 2018, the Transgender Persons Act 2019 and Supriyo 2023. The intersectional caution: queer movements have been savarna and metropolitan, so **Pride is the most visible and least representative slice**.
notes.103: Disability is under-counted: Census 2011 reported 2.21% while WHO and the World Bank put the figure at 15 to 20%. The gap reflects a politics of measurement as well as measurement error. Remember the social model, and the RPWD Act's 21 categories and 4% job reservation. The slide's closing demand: disability as a **baseline design requirement**.
notes.104: Language gatekeeps state employment, courts and education, and English fluency tracks caste, class and region almost perfectly, which the slide calls the silent reservation. Anti-Hindi agitations, the Eighth Schedule's 22 languages and the three-language formula keep the politics live. Federalism is the **constitutional containment device**.
notes.105: Class never travels alone, yet it has its own logic: capital accumulation, the wage relation and the agrarian question. About 90% of the workforce is informal, and the top 1% hold about 40% of wealth. The slide's political question has a clear answer: **universal programmes require intersectional targeting** to be universal.
notes.106: Migration and statelessness make the migrant both the engine of the urban economy and its most exposed citizen. Note the figures: 450 million internal migrants in Census 2011, about 10 million walking home in 2020, and 1.9 million excluded from Assam's final NRC. Domicile and citizenship differ, so welfare **does not follow the worker**.
notes.107: Use the six steps as the course's toolkit: diagnose, disaggregate, read recognition with redistribution, centre affected voice beyond tokenism, resist single-axis solutions, and build for decades. Each step names a failure it prevents. Keep the closing thought: working at the margin is **working on the structure that creates it**.
notes.108: Adivasis are 8.6% of the population but bear about 40% of development-induced displacement, and only about 25% have been rehabilitated. FRA titles are approved in large numbers, yet only about 13% of the area claimed as community forest rights is recognised. For programmes in tribal districts, **gram sabha consent and verified FPIC are non-negotiable**.
notes.109: India has the world's third-largest Muslim population. Sachar found Muslims worse off than SCs on several indicators, with 4.9% of central government jobs against a 14% population share. Treat Sachar-era data as a floor, and triangulate with NFHS-6 and NFHS-5. Remember that **'minority' covers very different communities**: Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists and Jains differ sharply.
notes.110: Start with the care economy: women spend 297 minutes a day on unpaid domestic and care work against 31 for men, a 9.6 times gap. Then note maternal mortality of 97 per 100,000 with sharp state variation, Kerala 19 and Assam 195. The slide's counter: disaggregating by sex is necessary but insufficient, so give **care, time and SRHR their own line items**.
notes.111: The legal position of queer and trans Indians has shifted since 2014, yet rights remain partial in practice. Learn the four rulings in order: NALSA 2014, Navtej 2018, the 2019 Act critiqued for district-magistrate certification, and Supriyo 2023 leaving marriage to Parliament. The open frontier is **horizontal civil rights**.
notes.112: The RPWD Act 2016 upgraded the law to 21 disabilities and a 4% job quota, yet only about 1.5% of central posts under the quota are filled. About 27% of disabled school-age children are out of school against about 3% generally. Use the **seven RPWD pillars** as an accessibility checklist, and consult DPOs from design stage.
notes.113: India has 22 Eighth Schedule languages, 780 recorded by the People's Linguistic Survey and 197 endangered per UNESCO. Hindi is official and English associate official, and the three-language formula keeps contestation alive. The practitioner rule: **design-stage multilingualism**, because translation as an afterthought loses nuance, especially in legal and rights education.
notes.114: The evidence says class compounds with caste. The top 1% wealth share was 40.5% in 2021, and 36% of below-poverty-line households are SC/ST against about 24% of the population. Programmes targeting by income reach a different population from those targeting by caste, so the best design **uses both**.
notes.115: The chart is illustrative, with edge thickness drawn from Sachar, NFHS-5, Census 2011 and the Xaxa Committee. Read it for the pattern: caste crossed with gender produces some of the sharpest deprivation, tribe crossed with religion is invisible in much policy data, and disability compounds every other vector but **is rarely tracked as an axis**.
notes.116: Registered PoA cases grew from about 28,000 in 1995 to about 64,000 in 2022, while the conviction rate stayed around 30 to 35% for two decades. Read the two series together. Rising registration beside a flat conviction rate points to **an implementation gap**, as the slide concludes.
notes.117: Use this as a two-part reading list: primary Indian sources and data on one side, major scholarly and literary works on the other. Start with Ambedkar's Writings and Speeches and the listed Constitution articles, then the surveys: NCRB, NFHS-5 and the Bihar tables. Match each source to **the section you are working on**.
notes.118: This slide gives the scholarly and literary shelf on its own. Read foundational thinkers first, then modern scholarship and literary voices. Pair a theory text such as Ambedkar or Rege with an empirical one such as **Thorat and Newman or Deshpande** so that argument and evidence arrive together.
notes.119: Learn the first glossary as definitions with owners: Crenshaw, Spivak, Fraser, Chakravarti. Note the Vector column, which shows how terms like Pasmanda sit across caste and religion. Check that you can state the difference between **varna and jati** from memory, since jati is the operative reality.
notes.120: The second glossary covers Acts and the vectors. Pay attention to entries that join vectors: Brahmanical patriarchy with sexuality, honour killing across caste, religion and gender, and endogamy as the master mechanism. Test yourself by explaining each term **without looking at the definition**.
notes.121: Read the chart as a headcount ratio by social group from NITI Aayog's 2023 National MPI. ST and SC groups carry rates roughly twice the national average, and Muslims similarly high. National aggregates **hide vertical inequalities**, which is why targeted reservation and welfare design exist.
notes.122: The chart shows reported deaths while cleaning sewers, septic tanks and manholes from 1993 to 2024, at 50 to 110 a year. The slide calls the numbers conservative and says over 95% of those who die are Dalits. Read it as **caste in its most violent material form**.
